lessons.title: Secondary dominants
explanation: Treat another chord as a brief tonic by giving it its own dominant. V/V in C is D major (or D7): the dominant of G, which is V. The F# is the leading tone of G, not a decorative sharp. MIT 21M.302 calls that tonicization: a visit, not a move of house.

Write a V/V that actually tonicizes. The next chord should be the one you treated as tonic — V, or a deceptive stand-in for it. A random D major that goes to F, or to E5, did not tonicize G. It was just a major triad. The accidental has to pay the visit.

Riffs reuse this as a chromatic shove into a goal chord. D-D7-G-C is still the grammar. A metal cell that throws a C# in to lean on D, then stays on D, is tonicizing D. If the C# never aims at a landing, it is not V of anything. Name the target or drop the label.
lessons.example: In C: D7 to G to C. F# leaned to G; G then did its dominant job toward C. Swap the G for an E5 that never arrives and you wrote a major chord, not a V/V.
lessons.whyItMatters: Secondary dominants are how chromaticism gets a job. Without a target, the sharp is only paint.

quiz.stem: A secondary dominant does which temporary job in a key?
quiz.correctAnswer: Treats another chord as a tonic by giving that chord its own dominant

distractors.text: Replaces the real tonic forever, which is already a modulation
distractors.rationale: Temporary is the point. A stay would be modulation.

distractors.text: Deletes all accidentals so every triad must remain diatonic
distractors.rationale: The accidental is how the borrowed dominant is spelled.

distractors.text: Names a power chord, because V/V is defined as a fifth without a third
distractors.rationale: V/V is a function label for a tonicizing dominant, not a dyad.

quiz.correctExplanation: Someone else's dominant, briefly. That is tonicization.
objectiveIds: Temporarily treat another chord as a tonic with its own dominant

quiz.stem: In C major, which spelling actually tonicizes V rather than adding a random major?
quiz.correctAnswer: D-F#-A-(C) going to G: F# is the leading tone of the target G

distractors.text: D-F-A going to E, with no F# and no G landing to confirm the visit
distractors.rationale: No leading tone of G, and no G. That D minor/major did not tonicize V.

distractors.text: E-G#-B going to C, which would be V/vi at best, not V/V
distractors.rationale: G# leans to A, not to G. Different target.

distractors.text: B-D-F with no accidental, because vii° already counts as V/V
distractors.rationale: vii° in C tonicizes C, not G. V/V needs the F# lean into G.

quiz.correctExplanation: F# toward G, then G. That is a V/V that paid the visit.
objectiveIds: Write a V/V that actually tonicizes, not a random major chord

quiz.stem: A riff throws C# then never lands on D. Diagnose the C# as:
quiz.correctAnswer: Not a V/V of D unless some D (or a stand-in) actually receives the lean

distractors.text: Automatically V/V, because any sharp is a secondary dominant by law
distractors.rationale: The label needs a target. A stray sharp is not V of something.

distractors.text: A modulation to C#, because hanging accidentals always move house
distractors.rationale: Hanging is not a new tonic. Modulation has to stay in a new key.

distractors.text: A plagal cadence, which is how secondary dominants are required to resolve
distractors.rationale: Plagal is IV-I. Secondary dominants resolve as dominants.

quiz.correctExplanation: No landing, no tonicization. Do not print V/D on a stray C#.
objectiveIds: Write a V/V that actually tonicizes, not a random major chord

lessons.title: Borrowed from the parallel
explanation: Borrow a chord from the parallel mode. In C major, take iv (F minor), bVI (Ab major), bIII (Eb), or bVII (Bb) from C minor. The tonic letter stays C. The color comes from the borrowed third or sixth. MIT 21M.302 treats that as mixture, not as a new key.

Predict the color. bVI in major is the dark slide a third below tonic: Ab in C, often as a chorus lift that feels heavier, not brighter. Minor iv under a major melody is the same borrow with a smaller footprint. Neither chord is a mistake that needs correcting back to IV or vi.

Riffs already do this. A major-key verse that hits Ab and Bb before C is mixing, not failing diatonicism. If the piece then stays in Ab, you have modulated. Mixture comes home. Name the borrow, name the return, and leave the color on the tape.
lessons.example: C major verse, chorus on Ab-Bb-C. Ab is bVI, Bb is bVII, C is still tonic. Same band's bridge that cadences in Ab and stays there is no longer mixture.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without mixture as a name, every borrowed iv looks like a wrong chord or a fake modulation.

quiz.stem: Modal mixture is the move of borrowing a chord from where?
quiz.correctAnswer: The parallel mode: same tonic, the other major or minor collection

distractors.text: A random distant key, which is already a modulation of tonic
distractors.rationale: Parallel keeps the tonic letter. A new tonic would be modulation.

distractors.text: The next species exercise, which supplies mixture as a cantus rule
distractors.rationale: Mixture is a harmonic borrow, not a counterpoint species.

distractors.text: The power-chord dictionary, because only dyads can be borrowed
distractors.rationale: You can borrow full triads and sevenths from the parallel.

quiz.correctExplanation: Same tonic, other mode. That is the borrow.
objectiveIds: Borrow a chord from the parallel mode

quiz.stem: In C major, a bVI or a minor iv is predicted to color the phrase how?
quiz.correctAnswer: Darker borrowed color from C minor, tonic still C, not a new home

distractors.text: Brighter, because any accidental raises the mood of the major key
distractors.rationale: bVI and iv lower pitches. The usual color is darker, not brighter.

distractors.text: As an automatic V/V, because Ab always tonicizes G in major
distractors.rationale: Ab as bVI is a borrowed triad, not by itself V of G.

distractors.text: As silence, because mixture is defined as deleting the tonic letter
distractors.rationale: The tonic stays. The borrowed chord is extra color on it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Ab or Fm in C major: parallel minor color, still C.
objectiveIds: Predict the color of a bVI or a minor iv in a major key

quiz.stem: A chorus in G major hits Eb then C minor then G. The honest label is:
quiz.correctAnswer: Mixture: bVI and iv borrowed from G minor, then a return to G

distractors.text: Modulation to Eb, because the first borrowed chord always becomes tonic
distractors.rationale: A visit to Eb color is not a stay in Eb unless the tonic actually moves.

distractors.text: A failed G major that must be rewritten as diatonic IV and vi
distractors.rationale: The borrow is the device. 'Fixing' it deletes the color.

distractors.text: Secondary dominants of G, which is what every flat triad means
distractors.rationale: Eb and Cm are mixture from G minor, not V/V machinery.

quiz.correctExplanation: Borrowed from the parallel, then home. Mixture, not a new key.
objectiveIds: Borrow a chord from the parallel mode

lessons.title: Changing tonic for good
explanation: Change tonic and mean it. A pivot chord belongs to both keys and lets you reassign jobs. A direct shift just starts writing in the new key. Either way, cadences and later phrases treat the new letter as home. MIT 21M.302 wants that stay, not a single chromatic shove.

Distinguish tonicization from modulation by what happens after the visit. V/V to V to I came home. A passage that cadences in G, writes new phrases in G, and does not treat C as tonic anymore has modulated. One secondary dominant is a visit. A stay is a move of house.

Riffs modulate too, often by direct shift: a half-step bump of the whole cell, or a chorus that lives a minor third away and never comes back. Do not invent a pivot that is not there. Do not call a four-bar tonicization a new key just to make the worksheet look chromatic.
lessons.example: Song in C: D7-G-C is tonicization of G, then home. Later the solo cadences in E minor and the next verse stays in E minor. That is a modulation. The D7 was not.
lessons.whyItMatters: If visit and stay use one word, you will rekey a song every time a secondary dominant winks.

quiz.stem: To modulate in the sense of this lesson you must:
quiz.correctAnswer: Change tonic and mean it, using a pivot or a direct shift that stays

distractors.text: Add one sharp as a secondary dominant, then cadence back in the old tonic
distractors.rationale: That is tonicization coming home, not a stay in a new key.

distractors.text: Borrow iv once, which is already defined as leaving the tonic forever
distractors.rationale: Mixture comes home. Modulation is the stay.

distractors.text: Delete the bass, because keys cannot change while a pedal is held
distractors.rationale: A pedal can sit under a key change. The tonic is the job, not the mute.

quiz.correctExplanation: New home, and later phrases treat it as home. Pivot or shove.
objectiveIds: Change tonic and mean it, with a pivot or a direct shift

quiz.stem: V/V to V to I, versus a passage that cadences in V and stays there, differs how?
quiz.correctAnswer: The first is a tonicization that comes home; the second is a modulation that stays

distractors.text: They are two names for mixture, which never involves a dominant at all
distractors.rationale: Mixture is a parallel borrow. This contrast is visit versus stay.

distractors.text: The first is already a modulation, because any F# rekeys the piece
distractors.rationale: F# in V/V is a visit to V, paid off by returning to I.

distractors.text: The second is only a pedal, because staying on V cannot be a tonic
distractors.rationale: If phrases treat V's letter as home, that letter is the new tonic.

quiz.correctExplanation: Come home versus stay. That is tonicization versus modulation.
objectiveIds: Distinguish a tonicization that comes home from a modulation that stays

quiz.stem: A chorus bumps the whole riff up a minor third and the rest of the song lives there. Diagnose:
quiz.correctAnswer: A direct-shift modulation: new tonic, meant, with no pivot required

distractors.text: Mixture, because a minor third is always a borrowed bIII that must return
distractors.rationale: If it never returns, the bIII color became the new home.

distractors.text: A failed V/V, which is the only legal way chromatic music may move
distractors.rationale: Direct shift is a legal modulation. It does not owe a secondary dominant.

distractors.text: Still the old key, because riffs are forbidden from changing tonic
distractors.rationale: Riffs modulate when later phrases treat the new letter as home.

quiz.correctExplanation: The song stayed in the new letter. That is modulation, pivot or not.
objectiveIds: Change tonic and mean it, with a pivot or a direct shift

lessons.title: Outside pitches with jobs
explanation: Give an outside pitch a job: approach, color, or new tonic. Approach is a chromatic step into a chord tone. Color is mixture or a chromatic mediant that still sits in the old key. New tonic is modulation. MIT 21M.302 wants the job named before anyone says 'color' as a shrug.

Rewrite a chromatic line that is only filling space. If the extra letters do not approach, do not color a stack, and do not aim at a stay, they are filler. Keep one job per letter. A walk C-C#-D is approach. Ab in C major as bVI is color. A cadence in E that stays is a new tonic.

Heavy riffs reuse all three jobs, often in one verse. A chromatic pickup into a power chord is approach. A borrowed bVI wall is color. A chorus that never returns is a new tonic. Do not flatten those into one word. The outside pitch still has to work for a living.
lessons.example: Fill: E-F-F#-G as a guitar run into G5 — F and F# approach. Color: the next chord is C minor in E major. New tonic: the bridge cadences in G and the outro stays there.
lessons.whyItMatters: Calling every accidental 'color' is how chromaticism becomes weather instead of voice leading.

quiz.stem: An outside pitch in this lesson should be given which kind of job?
quiz.correctAnswer: Approach a chord tone, color the present key, or become a new tonic

distractors.text: Any job at random, because accidentals are exempt from function talk
distractors.rationale: The point is to hire the pitch, not to waive analysis.

distractors.text: Only a rest, because pitches outside the key must not sound
distractors.rationale: They sound. They need a job: approach, color, or new tonic.

distractors.text: Only a power chord, because chromatic letters cannot join triads
distractors.rationale: Outside pitches join lines and stacks constantly. Name the job.

quiz.correctExplanation: Three jobs. Approach, color, new tonic. Pick one.
objectiveIds: Give an outside pitch a job: approach, color, or new tonic

quiz.stem: A guitar fills a bar with C-Db-D-Eb-E and none of those letters aim at a stack. Diagnose:
quiz.correctAnswer: Filler: rewrite so each chromatic letter approaches, colors, or rekeys

distractors.text: Perfect mixture, because any run of flats is a borrowed parallel chord
distractors.rationale: Mixture is a borrowed stack with a tonic that stays, not a shapeless run.

distractors.text: A modulation to Db, which every run that starts on C must perform
distractors.rationale: A run is not a stay. Modulation needs a new home that later phrases keep.

distractors.text: Species first-species, which requires chromatic filling on every beat
distractors.rationale: First species is mostly diatonic consonance, not a chromatic dump.

quiz.correctExplanation: No approach, no color stack, no new tonic. Rewrite the filler.
objectiveIds: Rewrite a chromatic line that is only filling space

quiz.stem: F# as a pickup into G5, Ab as bVI in C, and a verse that stays in E after a cadence: assign jobs.
quiz.correctAnswer: Approach, color, and new tonic — three different outside-pitch jobs

distractors.text: All color, which is the only legal word for any accidental in a riff
distractors.rationale: Color is one job. Approach and new tonic are the other two.

distractors.text: All V/V, because every sharp or flat is a secondary dominant of G
distractors.rationale: Ab as bVI is mixture. A stay in E is modulation. Only some F#s tonicize.

distractors.text: All passing tones, because chromatic letters may only walk by step
distractors.rationale: Passing is one approach path. Color chords and new tonics are other jobs.

quiz.correctExplanation: Pickup approaches. bVI colors. Stay rekeys. Three jobs, three labels.
objectiveIds: Give an outside pitch a job: approach, color, or new tonic

lessons.title: Lowered second as a color
explanation: Approach the dominant from the side. A Neapolitan is a major triad on the lowered second, often in first inversion (N6): in C, Db-F-Ab with F in the bass, going to G. An Italian augmented sixth (It+6) is typically Ab-C-F# in C, the outer gap an augmented sixth that wants to open to G-G.

Spell so the resolution is honest. Neapolitan: Db is the lowered 2, not C# (which would lean up as a leading tone). It+6: write Ab and F#, not G#, so the two letters can slide outward to G. MIT 21M.302 cares about those spellings because the lean is in the letters.

Treat both as color that later music can steal without the whole grammar. A riff that hits Db major before a G wall is using Neapolitan color even if no chorale inner voice is present. If there is no dominant to approach, say so: then Db is just a neighboring major, not N6.
lessons.example: In C: F in the bass, Db and Ab above, then G-B-D. N6 to V. Same chorus later slams Db5 to C5 with no G: neighboring color, not a Neapolitan approach.
lessons.whyItMatters: Wrong spelling hides the lean. Fake N6 labels hide that no dominant was ever approached.

quiz.stem: A Neapolitan or an Italian augmented sixth is used here to:
quiz.correctAnswer: Approach the dominant from a lowered second or an augmented sixth

distractors.text: Replace the tonic forever, which already names a modulation to bII
distractors.rationale: These are predominants into V, not a new home by default.

distractors.text: Delete the fifth from every chord so only power chords remain
distractors.rationale: They are spelled triads or sixth-chords, not a ban on fifths.

distractors.text: Name any chromatic mediant, because all flat chords are Neapolitan
distractors.rationale: Neapolitan is specifically bII. Mediants are a different relation.

quiz.correctExplanation: Side door into V. Lowered 2, or the augmented-sixth stretch.
objectiveIds: Approach the dominant from a lowered second or an augmented sixth

quiz.stem: In C, which spelling of N6 or It+6 keeps the resolution honest?
quiz.correctAnswer: Db-F-Ab (F in bass) to G, or Ab-C-F# opening outward to G-G

distractors.text: C#-E-G# to G, using C# so the lowered second leans up as a leading tone
distractors.rationale: C# would want D. Neapolitan is Db, a lowered 2 that is a color into V.

distractors.text: Ab-C-G# to G, writing G# instead of F# so both letters share a name
distractors.rationale: G# would lean to A. The augmented sixth needs F# sliding to G.

distractors.text: D-F-Ab to C, which is ii diminished, not a side-door predominant
distractors.rationale: That stack does not approach V as N6 or It+6.

quiz.correctExplanation: Db not C#, F# not G#. The letters have to be able to lean into V.
objectiveIds: Spell a Neapolitan or It+6 so the resolution is honest

quiz.stem: A riff hits Db5 then C5 and never takes G. You should predict the label is:
quiz.correctAnswer: Neighbor color, not N6, because no dominant was approached

distractors.text: N6 anyway, because any Db in C major is Neapolitan by worksheet law
distractors.rationale: N6 is a predominant into V. No V, no N6.

distractors.text: It+6, because power chords automatically spell augmented sixths
distractors.rationale: A fifth-stack is not Ab-C-F#. Different object.

distractors.text: A modulation to G that the missing G still somehow confirms
distractors.rationale: You cannot confirm a dominant that never sounded.

quiz.correctExplanation: No V, no Neapolitan job. Db5-C5 is color next door.
objectiveIds: Approach the dominant from a lowered second or an augmented sixth

lessons.title: Pattern that transposes itself
explanation: Transpose a pattern so the sequence is the form. A two-chord cell, or a bass step plus a sixth, repeats at a fixed interval: down a second, down a fifth, up a step. The pattern is the story. MIT 21M.301/302 drills falling-fifth sequences because they walk function without a new idea every bar.

Predict where it must break to cadence. Sequences do not close; they carry. To cadence you stop transposing, take a real PD-D-T (or whatever close this music uses), and let a phrase end. If you sequence all the way into the double bar, you wrote a tunnel, not a close.

Riffs sequence constantly. A guitar cell that drops two frets three times is a sequence. It still has to break for a chorus landing. Do not force each transposing copy to be a new T-PD-D. The copy is the form. Save function talk for the break.
lessons.example: C-Am-F-Dm-Bb-Gm, then stop: G-C. The copies fell by a step. The G-C is the break that cadences. Keep copying into Bb-Gm-Ab-Fm and you never land.
lessons.whyItMatters: If the copy is treated as a new progression every bar, you will 'fix' the sequence and destroy the form.

quiz.stem: A harmonic sequence is formed when you do which operation to a cell?
quiz.correctAnswer: Transpose the pattern so the copy-and-shift is the form itself

distractors.text: Cadence after every bar so each copy is a closed authentic pair
distractors.rationale: Cadence is what breaks a sequence. The copies carry, they do not close.

distractors.text: Delete the bass so only upper parts may repeat a shape
distractors.rationale: Bass often carries the interval of transposition. Do not mute it.

distractors.text: Borrow one parallel chord and call that single borrow a sequence
distractors.rationale: Mixture is one borrow. Sequence is a transposed repetition.

quiz.correctExplanation: Copy the cell at a fixed interval. The copies are the form.
objectiveIds: Transpose a pattern so the sequence is the form

quiz.stem: Where must a sequence break if the phrase is going to cadence?
quiz.correctAnswer: Stop transposing, take a real close, and let the copies end

distractors.text: Never: a true sequence is defined as cadencing on every copy
distractors.rationale: Copies carry. Cadence is the break, not the repetition.

distractors.text: After exactly one bar, because sequences are illegal past a single cell
distractors.rationale: Sequences can run several copies. They still have to break to close.

distractors.text: By inventing a V-I under each copy so function never has to stop
distractors.rationale: Pasting V-I on every copy hides the sequence and still may not close.

quiz.correctExplanation: Break the copy. Then cadence. The tunnel does not close itself.
objectiveIds: Predict where a sequence must break to cadence

quiz.stem: A riff drops a two-fret cell three times then slams a G5-C5 landing. Diagnose the G5-C5 as:
quiz.correctAnswer: The break where the sequence stopped transposing so a close could happen

distractors.text: Just another copy, because landings are forbidden to leave the pattern
distractors.rationale: The landing is the break. That is how sequences cadence.

distractors.text: A modulation to a new tonic on every dropped copy of the cell
distractors.rationale: Transposition of a cell is not automatically a key change.

distractors.text: A species error, because sequences may only be written in first species
distractors.rationale: Sequence is a harmonic form. Species is a line gym.

quiz.correctExplanation: Three copies, then a close. The G5-C5 is the predicted break.
objectiveIds: Predict where a sequence must break to cadence
